content_html_sanitized:
It is easy to find examples of prohibitionist propaganda in one of the “usual suspects”, like the New York Post or the UK’s Daily Mail, but these examples are from the widely respected National Geographic, which I started reading almost eighty years ago.

 The recent problem begins with the title;5  Scientific Findings That Change What We Know About Cannabis.” byAllie Yang, December 19, 2024

First, these are not “recent”.

Second, they are not “scientific findings”.

Third, they do not “change what we know.” Etc.

“As legal restrictions loosen, scientists are investigating long held beliefs that cannabis has few side effects and can effectively relieve pain.”

Notice that it begins with “As legal restrictions loosen…”  

Actually, marijuana remains a Schedule 1 drug at the Federal level, meaning that it has no medical use and research remains difficult, even though in December of 2022 President Biden did sign a law to make it easier. But none of the “recent scientific findings” Nat Geo cites are post 2022.

 See A new US law aims to ease access for researchers who want to study potential medical uses of marijuana. 

Perhaps NatGeo means that now that fewer people are being arrested we need to print more pseudo science.

This is a consistent theme in prohibitionist propaganda, implying that we know more about the dangers of marijuana that we all thought was harmless because of those lying legalizers.

Could it begin with “As marijuana moves out of the black market and Federal restrictions on marijuana research are loosened??

Other than that, the Federal restrictions have not changed at all, just the enforcement levels. And what about restrictions on medical research?

See Frequently Asked Questions about Conducting Research with Cannabis and Hemp

 “Long held beliefs?” What about a little history?

How did ”Marihuana”, originally the legal name in the US for Cannabis, end up a ‘Schedule 1’ along with heroin and LSD. What exactly does that mean? Is that a “scientific” term? And how did that happen?

When was it put in Schedule 1? And how did it end up with a Mexican slang term?

The great “scientist” who put it there was Nixon’s Attorney General, John Mitchell, who went to prison for his role in the Watergate burglary cover up. He placed marijuana in this category in 1972 as part of the ranking or “scheduling” of all drugs under the 1970 Controlled Substances Act. Schedule I drugs are deemed to have no medical use and a high potential for abuse. Cannabis has been there ever since.”

Why doesn’t NatGeo think we should know that?

Also back in 1972, The Shafer Commission, The National Commission on Marihuana and Drug Abuse recommended that it be decriminalized. Of course, Nixon rejected the recommendation of his own commission and the Federal law has not changed.

But recently, as in “the latest research”, researchers listening to Nixon’s infamous tapes found that he knew that marijuana wasn’t “particularly dangerous.”

See Richard Nixon Privately Admitted Marijuana Was 'Not Particularly Dangerous'

How would we measure pain relief to know whether to arrest someone? Or why? Are people really lying when they say that they hurt less? What about anorexia (remember the munchies), or nausea from cancer chemotherapy?

 From last October: “As More People with Cancer Use Medical Cannabis, Oncologists Face Questions They Struggle to Answer.

It is still a serious problem.

What about AIDS? Remember it was the San Francisco AIDS patients who got the first “medical marijuana” laws passed in 1996

See  1996 California Proposition 215

“Despite how many Americans use cannabis—now about one in five—there has historically been a gap in our scientific understanding of its health effects. But as policies against the drug loosen, we’re starting to learn more than ever about cannabis.” 

“Policies against the drug”? We learn more by arresting fewer people? How would that work? Did the marijuana reform movement block research? Or was it the Federal Government?

“You might think we know a lot about cannabis….Conventional wisdom holds that cannabis offers a safe, natural alternative to pharmaceuticals for treating pain, nausea, muscle spasms, appetite, and post-traumatic stress disorder.”

Oh, no! Not the dreaded “conventional wisdom”!?

Is cannabis less safe than pharmaceuticals? How many people have died in the last year after taking cannabis, (roughly 0) compared with over the counter medications, (roughly 17,000) available without a prescription at your corner drug store.

Every year in the United States, NSAID, aspirin,etc, use is attributed to approximately 100,000 hospitalizations and 17,000 deaths.

Isn’t cannabis “natural”? When cannabis was first banned under Federal law by the Marihuana Tax Act of 1937, almost no one except jazz musicians of color, and disreputable whites who liked jazz used reefer.

Sixty years later in 1997, one year after California’s Prop 215, the first medical marijuana initiative, there were roughly 600,000 arrests for marijuana, roughly 85% for simple possession. In 2025, there’s rarely been a mention of the over 30 million arrests since Nixon’s lawyer made a medical decision. (Have there been studies on the health benefits of being arrested? Seriously. There are still roughly 200,000 Americans arrested every year on marijuana charges. Disproportionately non white, of course.

2. “Cannabis isn't harmless.”

Harmless? This isn’t a recent “scientific finding”. This is the classic logical fallacy “straw man argument”.

Nothing is harmless for everyone, in all doses, and under all circumstances. But how does it compare with other drugs, like alcohol, tobacco, or over the counter medicines like aspirin?

“Cannabis certainly isn’t dangerous in the same way as opioids are, Deborah Hasin, an epidemiologist who has researched cannabis, told Landau in a March 2024 story. Still, Hasin says, it “can have a lot of other consequences to both physical and psychological health.”

 Alcohol? Facts About U.S. Deaths from Excessive Alcohol Use

1. Excessive alcohol use is a leading preventable cause of death in the United States.

2. About 178,000 people die from excessive drinking each year.

3. These deaths occur from both drinking alcohol over several years or drinking too much on one occasion.

Tobacco? “Cigarette smoking causes about one of every five deaths in the United States each year.1,6 Cigarette smoking is estimated to cause more than 480,000 deaths annually (including deaths from secondhand smoke)” CDC. But tobacco use by both adults and adolescents has fallen for decades without arresting millions of Americans. Youth Tobacco Product Use at a 25-Year Low, Yet Disparities Persist

 3. Cases of a rare syndrome related to cannabis use are rising.

“Then there’s an even more unusual downside to regular cannabis use: cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS). The condition, first described in 2004, involves reoccurring episodes of nausea, vomiting, and severe abdominal pain.”

Recent research? First described in 2004? How time flies.

And it would seem to be “heavy”, not “regular” use that is a risk factor. I am happy to say that I don't think that I personally know anyone who has this problem, and I do know a lot of cannabis users.

“Ironically, what made this disorder so puzzling was that medical professionals really knew all along that cannabis is an antiemetic.”

Emphasis added! Wow!

Now that is something that I absolutely agree with!

Think about that. As cancer and AIDS patients vomited their guts out, oncologists, the AMA, the FDA, the DEA, all knew that just a few puffs could stop the agony and even save lives. Indeed. I have met many cancer survivors who told me that they would have died, had they not been able to get illegal cannabis. If an individual did what the politicians and the medical profession did, they would have been charged with “manslaughter”.

Four. CANNABIS CAN AFFECT YOUR HEART

Possibly. As the number of cannabis users increases over time, the quality of the research that can be done will also increase, but that is of value only if it is used for public health purposes and not for prohibitionist propaganda.

The study cited here appears to be thorough, and it would appear to demonstrate that heavy cannabis use over time increases the risks. As legal cannabis becomes more readily available it seems likely that the risks can be reduced by reducing smoking in favor of vaporizing and edibles, and a better understanding of complementary cannabinoids and terpenes. However, it would be impossible to reduce whatever these risks may be in a black market drug.

See Exposure time to antidepressants was associated with a higher risk of sudden cardiac death, and linked to how long the person had been exposed to antidepressants.

And “I’m a cardiologist — this over prescribed drug taken by millions of people is toxic for your heart”

 5. WHAT’S IN A NAME? FOR CANNABIS STRAINS, LESS THAN YOU THINK

“One of the keys to creating a responsible future for the industry requires accurate naming…”

Again, this is the latest research? This is truly ironic. Until cannabis was completely legalized in some location, it was virtually impossible to know what it really was. Indeed, was it actually cannabis? Or was it “synthetic cannabis”? FNot actually genuine cannabis but a dangerous chemical sprayed on something leafy?

Our ignorance about cannabis is almost entirely a result of cannabis prohibition. Contraband has no quality controls. Serious research is impossible.

No, cannabis isn’t harmless. Nothing is harmless for everyone, at every dose and in every circumstance.

But neither is marijuana prohibition. Aside from thirty million plus Americans arrested, (not mentioned here, of course) creating an enormous black market with related violence and promotion of many more dangerous drugs (conveniently labeling marijuana a “gateway drug”), depriving sick and dying patients of relief from their pain and suffering and the ability to at least die in peace. What is the latest research that would tell me about that?

 This article isn’t about “recent scientific findings” It is a complete misrepresentation of the history of the legal battles about the regulatory status of cannabis since 1937. In short, it is typical of why I decided that MarijuanaNews.com is sadly still necessary.

See Cannabis Research Data Shows How US Funding Focuses On Harms of Drug

 Finally, let me emphasize that my quarrel is not with the author, about whom I know nothing, but with the editors of National Geographic, which I have read and respected for almost eighty years.

 As a further demonstration of that failure, NatGeo ran a similar piece on March 24 of last year:Do you smoke weed recreationally? Here's what experts want you to knowby Meryl Davids Landau March 22, 2024

 It begins with one of the oldest of the Prohibitionist cliches:“Today’s cannabis strains are not your grandma’s weed—and they may be impacting your mental health, heart health, and more.”

Well, my grandma didn’t smoke anything, but I’m old enough to be almost anyone’s grandpa, and, as has been said before, the 60s were not about a placebo.

We got high, and it wasn’t very difficult, even though we didn’t really know what we were smoking because it was contraband.Plus THC wasn’t discovered until 1964 and they didn’t tell us in Texas.

Since there was no way of knowing the potency of contraband cannabis, there has never been a standard dose, we adjusted accordingly. The stronger the weed, the smaller the dose.

Now, let me demonstrate the difference between 5%THC and 15%THC:

Raise your finger and thumb to your lips. That’s 5%. Repeat. That’s 10%. Repeat. That’s 15%.

By the way, 15% seems to be typical for “legal” cannabis in jurisdictions where it can be tested, because it is difficult and expensive to grow anything much stronger.

Now, if you’re not too stoned, or coughing too much, let’s continue, and consider why the contraband culture that still surrounds cannabis encourages higher THC weed.

It’s important to understand the economics of contraband: Iron law of Prohibition

First, if you are buying by weight and cannot really know what you are buying, or when you will be able to “score” again, you will want the strongest available. And for young men, the largest market, it would be Primo! Status!

Prohibition created the current culture. I may or may not have smoked “Acapulco Gold” back in the sixties, but, actually, there may never have been any such thing, because it was contraband, but it really is “legendary.”

The accuracy of the measurement of any “average” depends on the “sampling.” That was not possible under prohibition.

On the other hand, consider the accuracy of the sampling of a large “liquor store.” They sell everything from 90% grain alcohol to wine punch with 5% alcohol. A small quantity of the former could be lethal, if you didn’t know what it was. My grandma didn’t drink that either. But the legal alcohol industry knows what is being sold.

But with cannabis, could “stronger” even be safer? For decades we were told that smoking was the real danger because tobacco smoke was clearly dangerous, so Prohibitionist propaganda focused on that to the point of absurdity.

For example, when the success of California’s Medical Marijuana Initiative, Proposition 215  in 1996, the then Drug Czar, General Barry McCaffrey convened a commission that produced a new Prohibitionist campaign based on the slogan, “No Medicine Is Smoked”, suppressing the obvious fact that cannabis does not have to be smoked.

From 1999 SeeProhibitionism After the IOM Report; Analysis by Richard Cowan Repeat After Me: No Medicine Is Smoked! No Medicine Is Smoked! No Medicine Is Smoked!

The key point is that prohibition does not make anything safer. In fact, it makes everything more dangerous, and clearly does not stop people from consuming cannabis. “Edibles” are one more example of that.

The problem with edibles, or the FDA approved THC pills, Marinol, sold as Dronabinol, is that there is great variability in how long it takes for it to take effect, and, obviously if you are vomiting, swallowing it might be impossible.

Nonetheless, a lot of people, especially older medical users, prefer edibles, but they need to be in standard sizes and potentcies. Prohibition made that impossible.

One more thing about edibles and prohibition. It’s common to see stories about children getting improperly stored or packaged edibles and then being rushed to the hospital by their frightened parents. However, there have been no reported deaths, thankfully.

 Meanwhile,  “According to the 2022 United States (US) Consumer Product Safety Commission's (CPSC) annual report on pediatric poisoning fatalities and injuries, unintentional poisoning from household consumer products results in an average of 31 deaths of children under five years of age each year.”

 If it’s marijuana and not fatal, it’s news. If it’s not marijuana, and it’s fatal?? From What Are Common Causes of Poisoning in Children? “Medicines are the most common cause of poisoning in children. Several medicines you or a family member are taking can be dangerous to children. Opioids and barbiturates are well-known dangers, but medicines for high blood pressure, mental health, and diabetes are also hazardous.”

Stop the presses! Literally.

Now, to be constructive, let me suggest a few topics for the “latest research.” From Trends in Cigarette Smoking Among United States Adolescents “Cigarette use declined markedly from 1991 to 2021 in all usage categories: ever, occasional, frequent, and daily (Table 1). Specifically, ever use significantly decreased from 70.1% in 1991 to 17.8% in 2021 (P<0.05), an almost 4-fold decline. Occasional use significantly decreased from 27.5% in 1991 to 3.8% in 2021 (P<0.05), a greater than 7-fold decline. Frequent use significantly decreased from 12.7% to 0.7% (P<0.05), a greater than 18-fold decline. Daily use declined from 9.8% in 1991 to 0.6% in 2021, a greater than 16-fold decline.”

 All of this was accomplished without arresting a single American for simply possessing the highly addictive killer gateway drug. Or, how does the level of cannabis use in America compare with The Netherlands, where it has been sold “over the counter” (and inalmost every town, not just in Amsterdam) for almost fifty years.

From Cannabis Use by Country 2024 (cannabis users as percent of population)

The Netherlands 10.2%

The United States 21.9%

This must be the “latest research” because… well, have you seen anything about this reported in the US media lately? Or in the last 50 years? (December 17, this year, will be the 50th anniversary of the opening of The Bulldog, the first coffee shop.)

Or this? Cannabidiol, CBD, was actually discovered in 1940 (the year I was born), and three years after the Marihuana Tax Act, but because it was just a part of “marihuana”, the evil jazz drug, no medical research was done on it for decades.

And it wasn’t until the parents of a little girl with epilepsy tried “medical marijuana” for her seizures, that it was discovered that CBD could greatly reduce the number of her seizures.

See Charlotte’s Web

Oh, yeah, think of the children! Or maybe not?

 Meanwhile in the UK:“We grew cannabis illegally for our son, it gave us hope when there was none’. Medical cannabis has been legal since 2018 but, with access restricted, desperate parents are turning to dealers to help their sick children

 Then, a few days ago, as I was writing this, Nat Geo ran an excellent story about the US government deliberately poisoning alcohol during alcohol prohibition back in the 1930s.“During Prohibition, the U.S. government added toxins to industrial alcohol, knowing it could kill. The result? A chemical war that targeted the poor and reshaped public trust.”

Please note that they simply use the term “Prohibition” without referring to alcohol, as is standard in American “journalism”. Using the term “Marijuana Prohibition” would be “double plus ungood.”

See “Newspeak”

 Which brought to mind a similar story about the Federal government poisoning marijuana back in the 1970s with the herbicide Paraquat.

See POISONOUS FALLOUT FROM THE WAR ON MARIJUANA

 Finally, I did a search for “marijuana prohibition” on Nat Geo’s website search function and the response was  “We couldn't find a match for "marijuana prohibition”.

 Thirty million arrests, and counting. Paraquat poisoning. The suppression of medical cannabis and creating an international black market for an endless supply of truly dangerous substances, and NatGeo has to warn us about what my grandmother didn’t smoke.

Iremember way back when the National Geographic reported from countries that weren’t quite yet civilized. Where are they when we really need them?

The editocracy of NatGeo has failed its readers.

And they are hardly alone. From yesterday’s MarijuanaNews.comWhy Does Newsweek Push Prohibitionist Propaganda?
